Πῶς, φημί, κύριε; γνώρισόν μοι. Ἄκουε, φησίν· ὁ μὲν πλούσιος ἔχει χρήματα πολλά, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὸν Κύριον πτωχεύει περισπώμενος περὶ τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτοῦ, καὶ λίαν μικρὰν ἔχει τὴν ἐξομολόγησιν καὶ τὴν ἔντευξιν πρὸς τὸν Κύριον, καὶ ἣν ἔχει, μικρὰν καὶ βληχρὰν καὶ ἄνω μὴ ἔχουσαν δύναμιν. ὅταν οὖν ἀναβῇ ὁ πλούσιος ἐπὶ τὸν πένητα καὶ χορηγήσῃ αὐτῷ τὰ δέοντα, πιστεύων ὅτι ὃ ἐργάσεται εἰς τὸν πένητα δυνήσεται τὸν μισθὸν εὑρεῖν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ—ὅτι ὁ πένης πλούσιός ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ἐντεύξει [καὶ τῇ ἐξομολογήσει,] καὶ δύναμιν μεγάλην ἔχει ἡ ἔντευξις αὐτοῦ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ— ἐπιχορηγεῖ οὖν ὁ πλούσιος τῷ πένητι πάντα ἀδιστάκτως· 6. ὁ πένης δὲ ἐπιχορηγούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ πλουσίου ἐντυγχάνει αὐτῷ, τῷ Θεῷ εὐχαριστῶν περὶ τοῦ διδόντος αὐτῷ. κἀκεῖνος ἔτι ἐπισπουδάζει περὶ τοῦ πένητος, ἵνα ἀδιάλειπτος γένηται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ· οἶδε γὰρ ὅτι ἡ ἔντευξις τοῦ πένητος προσδεκτή ἐστι καὶ πλουσία πρὸς τὸν Θεόν. 7. ἀμφότεροι οὖν τὸ ἔργον τελοῦσιν· ὁ μὲν πένης ἐργάζεται τὴν ἔντευξιν ἐν ᾗ πλουτεῖ, [ἣν ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου·] ταύτην ἀποδίδωσι τῷ Κυρίῳ τῷ ἐπιχορηγοῦντι αὐτῷ. καὶ ὁ πλούσιος ὡσαύτως τὸν πλοῦτον ὃν ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἀδιστάκτως παρέχει τῷ πένητι. καὶ τοῦτο ἔργον μέγα ἐστὶ καὶ δεκτὸν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ὅτι συνῆκεν ἐπὶ τῷ πλούτῳ αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰργάσατο εἰς τὸν πένητα ἐκ τῶν δωρημάτων τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ ἐτέλεσε τὴν διακονίαν τοῦ Κυρίου ὀρθῶς. 8. παρὰ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις οὖν ἡ πτελέα δοκεῖ καρπὸν μὴ φέρειν, καὶ οὐκ οἴδασιν οὐδὲ νοοῦσιν ὅτι, ἐὰν ἀβροχία γένηται, ἡ πτελέα ὕδωρ ἔχουσα τρέφει τὴν ἄμπελον, καὶ ἡ ἄμπελος ἀδιάλειπτον ἔχουσα ὕδωρ διπλοῦν τὸν καρπὸν δίδωσι, καὶ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς πτελέας. οὕτω καὶ οἱ πένητες ἐντυγχάνοντες πρὸς τὸν Κύριον ὑπὲρ τῶν πλουσίων

translation.text:
For to this end the Master has made you rich[1], that you might carry out these ministries for him; it is far better to buy such fields [and estates] and houses, which you will find in your city when you arrive in it. This luxury is good and cheerful, having no grief nor fear, but having joy. So do not practice the luxury of the nations; for it is unprofitable for you, the servants of God. Rather practice your own luxury, in which you are able to rejoice. For all luxury of this kind is profitable. But the luxury of the nations is bitter and harsh. This parable, then, is set before the servants of God, for the poor and the rich.

‘How so, sir?’ I say. ‘Make it known to me.’ ‘Listen,’ he says: ‘The rich man has much money, but toward the Lord he is poor, being distracted about his wealth, and he has very little confession and intercession toward the Lord; and what he has is small and feeble, and has no power to go up above. When, therefore, the rich man goes to the needy and supplies him with what is necessary, believing that what he does for the needy he will be able to find as his wage from God—for the needy is rich in intercession [and in confession], and his intercession has great power with God—the rich man supplies the needy with everything without doubting. And the needy, being supplied by the rich, intercedes for him, giving thanks to God on behalf of the one who gives to him. And that one is still more eager concerning the needy, so that he may be unceasing in his life; for he knows that the intercession of the needy is acceptable and abundant with God. Therefore both complete the work: the needy performs the intercession in which he is rich, [which he received from the Lord;] this he renders to the Lord for the one who supplies him. And likewise the rich man without doubting provides to the needy the wealth which he received from the Lord. And this is a great work and acceptable with God, because he understood concerning his wealth and worked for the needy out of the gifts of the Lord and fulfilled the Lord’s ministry rightly. Therefore, among people the elm seems not to bear fruit; and they do not know nor understand that[2], if there should be a drought, the elm, having water, nourishes the vine, and the vine, having unceasing water, gives double fruit, both for itself and for the elm. In the same way also the needy[b][a][14][13][12][11][10][9][8][7][6][5][4][3], interceding with the Lord on behalf of the rich...

footnotes.text: "and estates" (καὶ κτήματα) appears bracketed in the Greek; some witnesses include it, others omit it.
ἐπιδημήσῃς can mean "be present as a resident/visitor"; here, the thought is of arriving again at one’s own city, an eschatological image in Hermas.
Hermas pointedly redefines "luxury" as joyful, fear-free generosity that stores up for life in the coming city.
The Greek δοῦλοι τοῦ Θεοῦ is rendered "slaves of God" to preserve the ownership-and-obedience nuance; "servants" is a smoother but less exact alternative.
"and in confession" (καὶ τῇ ἐξομολογήσει) is bracketed; the phrase may be a scribal addition or gloss.
ἔντευξις is a specific term for petitionary approach/intercession; alternatives are "petition" or general "prayer."
The clause likely means the needy person is sustained continually by the rich man’s care. Some take it of the rich man’s own constancy in doing good.
"Abundant with God" could also be translated "rich toward God," preserving the idiom πλουσία πρὸς τὸν Θεόν.
"Ministry" (διακονία) here is not a formal office but the service assigned by the Master, fulfilled in almsgiving.
The elm-and-vine image explains the mutual benefit: the elm stores/nourishes with water; the vine yields fruit for both itself and the elm.

The Greek here is difficult; the subject of "thrown to the ground it is rotten and bears little" is not explicit in the preserved text, but likely contrasts transient worldly luxury with enduring Christian "luxury."
"which he received from the Lord" is bracketed in the Greek and may reflect a textual variant.
μισθός is rendered "wage" to retain the remuneration metaphor; "reward" is an alternative.
"the nations" translates ἔθνη; "Gentiles" is an alternative. Hermas contrasts pagan luxury with Christian use of wealth.
Or 'in which you are able to give; but when it is thrown to the ground it bears rotten and little fruit.'.
Or 'unhesitatingly provides to the needy'.

The term denotes costly living. Hermas redeploys it ironically for almsgiving; "luxury" keeps the rhetorical edge.
Common sense fits the metaphor of laying up acquisitions for the future city.
In context of fields and houses, "estates" captures landed property; bracketed as a textual variant.
The verb means to be present in/return to a place as a visitor or resident; "arrive" is idiomatic and neutral.
Paired with "good" to describe a joy-filled kind of luxury; "cheerful" fits the tone.
Hermas contrasts believers with the nations; "the nations" keeps the Jewish-Christian idiom without over-reading ethnicity.
Economic metaphor aligns with discourse on wealth; "unprofitable" matches the warning to God’s slaves.
Project default: retain "slaves" where the ownership/service relation to God is salient.
General term for poor; contrasted with πλούσιος. Kept as "poor" for clarity.
πένης often denotes one who works yet is needy. Rendering as "needy" distinguishes it from πτωχός.
Technical term for a petitionary approach on behalf of another; "intercession" captures the mediated aspect.
In early Christian usage often confession of sins and praise. In Hermas' penitential setting, "confession" is apt.
Preserves retributive imagery of remuneration from God for works done for the needy.
Carries both cognitive and volitional firmness; "without doubting" fits Hermas’ emphasis on single-mindedness.
Denotes earnest concern; "is eager" renders the ongoing care of the rich for the needy.
Adverbial nuance in phrase about sustaining life; "without cease" mirrors the Greek lexical form.
Conventional cultic-prayer term; "acceptable" aligns with the idiom "acceptable to God."
Genitive/prepositional phrase indicates abundance in God’s presence; "abundant with God" keeps idiomatic freshness.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render as "Master" to preserve household-lord nuance distinct from "Lord" (κύριος).
theological_decisions.rationale: The passage frames God as the one who enriched believers and assigns ministries. "Master" sustains the parable’s service language.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Keep "luxury" and let Hermas redefine it as generous use of wealth for almsgiving and eschatological investment.
theological_decisions.rationale: Avoids flattening Hermas’ ironic rhetoric; he contrasts pagan luxury with a Christian "luxury" that is joyful and fear-free.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Render ἔντευξις as "intercession" and ἐξομολόγησις as "confession."
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas links the poor person’s spiritual wealth to mediated prayer and penitence; "intercession" + "confession" preserves this texture.
Hermas uses a remuneration metaphor: what is done for the needy will be paid back by God. "Wage" keeps the earthy economic feel.
Hermas often speaks of the eschatological city metaphorically. Retaining "city" preserves the allegory and avoids over-interpretation.

theological_decisions.issue: Subject of ἵνα ἀδιάλειπτος γένηται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Refer the pronoun to the needy person, i.e., the rich continues caring so that the needy may be sustained continually in life.
alternative_readings: Refer to the rich man’s constancy in generous living
theological_decisions.rationale: Nearest antecedent is the needy person; the care’s aim is his ongoing sustenance. This fits the reciprocal logic of the parable.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Interpret elm (apparently fruitless) as the rich, and vine as the needy; the needy’s intercessions nourish the rich to produce double fruit.
alternative_readings: Elm as the needy; vine as the rich (reversed)
theological_decisions.rationale: Immediate context explicitly frames the parable as for rich and poor; the vine’s double fruit for itself and the elm maps to the poor’s prayer benefiting both.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: "Without doubting" to foreground Hermas’ concern with double-mindedness.
theological_decisions.rationale: The moral discourse in Hermas frequently targets doubt/double-mindedness; this choice brings that lexical thread into view.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Bracketed phrases retained in square brackets in English where indicated in the Greek source.
theological_decisions.rationale: Signals to readers where the Greek witness is uncertain or has variants without adjudicating them at this stage.

translation.text:
…they make their wealth complete, and in turn the rich, by supplying the poor with the things they need, make their souls complete[a].

9. Thus both become partners in the work of righteousness. Therefore the one who does these things will not be abandoned by God, but will be inscribed in the books of the living[b].

10. Blessed are those who have and understand that they are made rich from the Lord; for those who think this way will be able to do some good.

Another parable.

1. He showed me many trees that had no leaves, but they seemed to me to be dry; for they were all alike. And he says to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see,” I say, “sir[c], that they are alike and dry.” Answering, he says to me, “These trees that you see are those who dwell in this age[d].”

2. “Why then, sir, are they as if dry and alike?” I say. “Because,” he says, “neither the righteous nor the sinners are visible in this age, but they are alike; for this age is winter for the righteous, and they are not visible while dwelling among sinners.”

3. “For just as in winter the trees, having cast off their leaves, are alike, and it is not apparent which are dry or which are living, so in this age neither the righteous nor the sinners are apparent, but all are alike.”

Another parable.

1. He showed me again many trees, some sprouting and others dry, and he says to me, “Do you see these trees?” “I see,” I say, “sir, some sprouting and others dry.”

2. “These trees that are sprouting,” he says, “are the righteous, who are about to dwell in the age to come; for the age to come is summer for the righteous, but winter for sinners. Therefore when the mercy of the Lord shines forth, then those serving God will be made manifest, and all will be made manifest.”

3. “For just as in summer the fruits of each tree become visible and are recognized for what they are, so also the fruits of the righteous will be visible, and all will be known, [those who are least] being flourishing in that age[e].”

4. “But the nations[f] and the sinners—like the dry trees you saw—will be found such, dry and fruitless in that age, and as …[g]”

footnotes.text: The verb πληροφορέω can mean to bring something to full measure or fulfillment. In this context it contrasts material 'wealth' with the 'soul,' each being made complete through mutual support.
On the motif, compare Exod 32:32–33; Ps 69:28; Dan 12:1. Hermas’s wording is plural ('books of the living'), not the singular 'book of life.'
Greek κύριε here is respectful address to the visionary guide; 'sir' avoids confusion with the divine title 'Lord.'
Greek αἰών denotes an age or epoch. Hermas contrasts the present age (winter) with the coming age (summer).
Some witnesses include the words 'οἱ ἐλάχιστοι ὄντες' ('even the least'), which would read, 'and all—even the least—will be known as flourishing in that age.'
ἔθνη is rendered 'the nations' rather than 'Gentiles' to retain a broad, non-technical sense.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bring to full measure / make complete
lexical_decisions.rationale: In Koine this verb can mean to bring something to fulfillment or completion (cf. 2 Tim 4:5). Here it fits the reciprocal image: the poor (by implication) and the rich each bring something to completion—wealth and soul. 'Make complete' is clear and preserves the metaphorical fullness.
Common sense of providing for needs; 'supplying' keeps the concrete economic imagery.
Context is material aid to the poor. 'Necessities' conveys required provisions rather than moral propriety.
'Partners' communicates mutual participation in a shared work without softening the ethical dimension.
δικαίου here is moral righteousness rather than abstract justice; 'work of righteousness' keeps Hermas’s ethical tone.
Stock biblical idiom; 'abandoned' is clear and weighty.

lexical_decisions.source_word: ἐπιγεγραμμένος εἰς τὰς βίβλους τῶν ζώντων
lexical_decisions.chosen: inscribed in the books of the living
alternatives: written in the book of the living
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the plural 'books' and the phrase 'of the living.' Echoes a known motif without collapsing to the singular 'book of life.'
'Blessed' preserves the beatitude register and gravity.
Cognitive grasp of the source of wealth is in view.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are made rich from the Lord
lexical_decisions.rationale: Passive divine agency; 'from the Lord' keeps the prepositional nuance (παρά).
Ethical mindset language common in early Christian paraenesis.
Keeps the concrete imagery of working good rather than abstract 'do good.'
Address is to the visionary’s guide, not to God. 'Sir' avoids conflation with the divine title 'Lord.'
Hermas contrasts present and coming 'ages' (temporal horizons), not cosmos vs. inhabited world. 'Age' preserves apocalyptic temporal frame.
Seasonal metaphor is explicit and vivid; 'winter'/'summer' are natural choices.
Light metaphor attached to mercy; 'shines out' keeps the concrete image.
While the verb connotes slavery, here the focus is on manifest service; 'serving God' reads smoothly without importing the full 'slave' metaphor.

lexical_decisions.chosen: fruits … are recognized what sort they are
alternatives: fruits … are found of what kind they are
fruits … are known what quality they are
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the evaluative nuance of ποταπός with the recognition verb.
Common arboreal/vitality metaphor; 'flourishing' fits the tree imagery and moral vigor.
'The nations' is the broad, non-technical term; 'Gentiles' risks later Christian ethnoreligious connotations not demanded here.
'Fruitless' aligns with the tree/fruit metaphor already in use.

theological_decisions.issue: Rendering κύριος (voc.) in dialogue with the angelic shepherd
theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Translate κύριε as 'sir' in this context
theological_decisions.rationale: The addressee is the visionary guide, not God. Using 'sir' prevents confusion with the divine title while preserving respectful address.

theological_decisions.issue: Eschatological contrast of αἰών (present vs. coming)
theological_decisions.rationale: Hermas contrasts temporal epochs (now vs. coming). 'Age' cleanly conveys this without cosmological overtones of 'world' or the opacity of 'aeon.'

theological_decisions.issue: 'Books of the living' vs. traditional 'book of life'
theological_decisions.rationale: The Greek is plural and says 'of the living.' Retaining it preserves Hermas’s diction and avoids importing later or different phrasing.

alternative_readings: 'Slaves of God' to emphasize doulos imagery
theological_decisions.rationale: Although the root can carry slavery imagery, here the focus is disclosure of allegiance ('those serving God'). 'Serving' communicates allegiance without over-specifying social metaphor.
Hermas’s paraenesis leans toward moral righteousness language; 'righteous' keeps the moral-ascetical tone and avoids juridical narrowing.

theological_decisions.chosen_reading: Take 'have' as material possession and render the clause, 'those who have and understand that from the Lord they are made rich'
alternative_readings: Generalize 'have' to any gift or capacity
theological_decisions.rationale: Context speaks of rich supplying necessities to the poor. Thus 'have' naturally refers to those possessing means.
'The nations' is the least anachronistic and widest term; Hermas’s contrast is moral (righteous vs. sinners) rather than insider/outsider to Israel.

review_passes.summary: The translation is excellent. It accurately captures the Greek source, maintains the appropriate register, and handles the textual fragment at the end perfectly. No changes are necessary.

source.text: τοῦ Θεοῦ. 9. εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ ἐπλούτισεν ὑμᾶς ὁ δεσπότης, ἵνα ταύτας τὰς διακονίας τελέσητε αὐτῷ· πολὺ βέλτιόν ἐστι τοιούτους ἀγροὺς ἀγοράζειν [καὶ κτήματα] καὶ οἴκους, οὓς εὑρήσεις ἐν τῇ πόλει σου, ὅταν ἐπιδημήσῃς εἰς αὐτήν. 10. αὕτη ἡ πολυτέλεια καλὴ καὶ ἱλαρά, λύπην μὴ ἔχουσα μηδὲ φόβον, ἔχουσα δὲ χαράν. τὴν οὖν πολυτέλειαν τῶν ἐθνῶν μὴ πράσσετε· ἀσύμφορον γάρ ἐστιν ὑμῖν τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ Θεοῦ· 11. τὴν δὲ ἰδίαν πολυτέλειαν πράσσετε, ἐν ᾗ δύνασ δίδωσιν, ἐρριμμένη δὲ χαμαὶ σαπρὸν καὶ ὀλίγον φέρει. αὕτη οὖν ἡ παραβολὴ εἰς τοὺς δούλους τοῦ Θεοῦ κεῖται, εἰς πτωχὸν καὶ πλούσιον. 5. Πῶς, φημί, κύριε; γνώρισόν μοι. Ἄκουε, φησίν· ὁ μὲν πλούσιος ἔχει χρήματα πολλά, τὰ δὲ πρὸς τὸν Κύριον πτωχεύει περισπώμενος περὶ τὸν πλοῦτον αὐτοῦ, καὶ λίαν μικρὰν ἔχει τὴν ἐξομολόγησιν καὶ τὴν ἔντευξιν πρὸς τὸν Κύριον, καὶ ἣν ἔχει, μικρὰν καὶ βληχρὰν καὶ ἄνω μὴ ἔχουσαν δύναμιν. ὅταν οὖν ἀναβῇ ὁ πλούσιος ἐπὶ τὸν πένητα καὶ χορηγήσῃ αὐτῷ τὰ δέοντα, πιστεύων ὅτι ὃ ἐργάσεται εἰς τὸν πένητα δυνήσεται τὸν μισθὸν εὑρεῖν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ—ὅτι ὁ πένης πλούσιός ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ἐντεύξει [καὶ τῇ ἐξομολογήσει,] καὶ δύναμιν μεγάλην ἔχει ἡ ἔντευξις αὐτοῦ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ— ἐπιχορηγεῖ οὖν ὁ πλούσιος τῷ πένητι πάντα ἀδιστάκτως· 6. ὁ πένης δὲ ἐπιχορηγούμενος ὑπὸ τοῦ πλουσίου ἐντυγχάνει αὐτῷ, τῷ Θεῷ εὐχαριστῶν περὶ τοῦ διδόντος αὐτῷ. κἀκεῖνος ἔτι ἐπισπουδάζει περὶ τοῦ πένητος, ἵνα ἀδιάλειπτος γένηται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ· οἶδε γὰρ ὅτι ἡ ἔντευξις τοῦ πένητος προσδεκτή ἐστι καὶ πλουσία πρὸς τὸν Θεόν. 7. ἀμφότεροι οὖν τὸ ἔργον τελοῦσιν· ὁ μὲν πένης ἐργάζεται τὴν ἔντευξιν ἐν ᾗ πλουτεῖ, [ἣν ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου·] ταύτην ἀποδίδωσι τῷ Κυρίῳ τῷ ἐπιχορηγοῦντι αὐτῷ. καὶ ὁ πλούσιος ὡσαύτως τὸν πλοῦτον ὃν ἔλαβεν ἀπὸ τοῦ Κυρίου ἀδιστάκτως παρέχει τῷ πένητι. καὶ τοῦτο ἔργον μέγα ἐστὶ καὶ δεκτὸν παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ, ὅτι συνῆκεν ἐπὶ τῷ πλούτῳ αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰργάσατο εἰς τὸν πένητα ἐκ τῶν δωρημάτων τοῦ Κυρίου καὶ ἐτέλεσε τὴν διακονίαν τοῦ Κυρίου ὀρθῶς. 8. παρὰ τοῖς ἀνθρώποις οὖν ἡ πτελέα δοκεῖ καρπὸν μὴ φέρειν, καὶ οὐκ οἴδασιν οὐδὲ νοοῦσιν ὅτι, ἐὰν ἀβροχία γένηται, ἡ πτελέα ὕδωρ ἔχουσα τρέφει τὴν ἄμπελον, καὶ ἡ ἄμπελος ἀδιάλειπτον ἔχουσα ὕδωρ διπλοῦν τὸν καρπὸν δίδωσι, καὶ ὑπὲρ ἑαυτῆς καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς πτελέας. οὕτω καὶ οἱ πένητες ἐντυγχάνοντες πρὸς τὸν Κύριον ὑπὲρ τῶν πλουσίων

translation.text: For to this end the Master has made you rich, that you might carry out these ministries for him; it is far better to buy such fields [and estates] and houses, which you will find in your city when you arrive in it. This luxury is good and cheerful, having no grief nor fear, but having joy. So do not practice the luxury of the nations; for it is unprofitable for you, the servants of God. Rather practice your own luxury, in which you are able to rejoice. For all luxury of this kind is profitable. But the luxury of the nations is bitter and harsh. This parable, then, is set before the servants of God, for the poor and the rich.

translation.text: ‘How so, sir?’ I say. ‘Make it known to me.’ ‘Listen,’ he says: ‘The rich man has much money, but toward the Lord he is poor, being distracted about his wealth, and he has very little confession and intercession toward the Lord; and what he has is small and feeble, and has no power to go up above. When, therefore, the rich man goes to the needy and supplies him with what is necessary, believing that what he does for the needy he will be able to find as his reward from God—for the needy is rich in intercession [and in confession], and his intercession has great power with God—the rich man supplies the needy with everything without hesitation. And the needy, being supplied by the rich, intercedes for him, giving thanks to God on behalf of the one who gives to him. And that one is still more eager concerning the needy, so that he may be unceasing in his life; for he knows that the intercession of the needy is acceptable and rich before God. Therefore both complete the work: the needy performs the intercession in which he is rich, [which he received from the Lord;] this he renders to the Lord for the one who supplies him. And likewise the rich man without hesitation provides to the needy the wealth which he received from the Lord. And this is a great work and acceptable with God, because he understood concerning his wealth and worked for the needy out of the gifts of the Lord and fulfilled the Lord’s ministry rightly. Therefore, among people the elm seems not to bear fruit; and they do not know nor understand that, if there should be a drought, the elm, having water, nourishes the vine, and the vine, having unceasing water, gives double fruit, both for itself and for the elm. In the same way also the needy, interceding with the Lord on behalf of the rich...

base_translation.text: For to this end the Master has made you rich, that you might carry out these ministries for him; it is far better to buy such fields [and estates] and houses, which you will find in your city when you arrive in it. This luxury is good and cheerful, having no grief nor fear, but having joy. So do not practice the luxury of the nations; for it is unprofitable for you, the slaves of God. Rather practice your own luxury, in which you are able to rejoice. For all luxury of this kind is profitable. But the luxury of the nations is bitter and harsh. This parable, then, is set before the slaves of God, for the poor and the rich.

translation.text:
The Master made you rich for this purpose: to carry out these services for him. It is far better to buy fields, estates, and houses like these. You will find them in your city when you arrive there. This kind of luxury is good and joyful. It brings no sorrow or fear, but joy.

So do not practice the luxury of the nations. It does no good for you, who are God’s servants. Instead, practice your own kind of luxury, in which you can rejoice. Every luxury of this kind is beneficial. But the luxury of the nations is bitter and harsh.

This parable, then, is for all God’s servants, both poor and rich.

translation.text:
“How is that so, sir?” I ask. “Explain it to me.”

“Listen,” he says. “A rich man has plenty of money, but he is poor in what concerns the Lord. His wealth distracts him, so he offers very little confession before God or prayer for others. What he does offer is weak and has no power to rise to God.

“But when the rich man helps a needy person and provides what he needs, he believes that God will reward him for it. The needy person is rich in prayer for others and in confession before God,[a] and his prayer has great power with God. So the rich man provides everything the needy person requires, without hesitation. In return, the needy person prays for him and thanks God for the one who helped him. Then the rich man becomes even more eager to care for the needy person, so that the needy person can continue living, because he knows that the needy person’s prayer is rich and acceptable before God.

“In this way, together they complete the work. The needy person offers the prayer in which he is rich—something he received from the Lord—and presents it to the Lord for the person who supports him. Likewise, the rich man freely shares with the needy person the wealth he received from the Lord. This is a great work that pleases God, because the rich man understood how he should use his wealth. He used the Lord’s gifts to help the needy and faithfully carried out the Lord’s service.

“To people, the elm appears to bear no fruit. But they do not know or understand that during a drought, when the elm has water, it nourishes the vine. Because the vine has a constant supply of water, it produces twice the fruit—fruit for itself and for the elm. In the same way, when needy people pray to the Lord for the rich...”
